opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the progress is going to be really fast, and I don't want to downplay that. But the picture some people have, where a model gets good enough to improve itself, and then a week later you have superintelligence, doesn't match what I've seen actually doing this research.

Part of it is that progress has always been bottlenecked by more than ideas. Even if you had an AI that was as good as the best researchers, you still have to run the experiments. You need compute, you need to train models, and a lot of these experiments take weeks or months. Having more smart researchers doesn't make a training run finish faster. So the cycle of having an idea, testing it, and learning from it has real physical constraints.

There's also the question of what "improving itself" means. When you look at how these breakthroughs have actually happened, like the reasoning paradigm, scaling test-time compute, it wasn't one brilliant insight that unlocked everything. It was a lot of incremental work, a lot of dead ends, and a lot of empirical grinding before something worked. I'd expect AI to speed that process up quite a bit, but speeding up isn't the same as going vertical overnight.

And then there's the deployment side. Even when capabilities exist, it takes time for them to diffuse into the world, for people to build infrastructure, for institutions to adapt. The real world adds friction.

So my view is that we'll see acceleration, maybe a lot of it, and things could look very different within a few years. But I think it'll look more like a steep, continuous curve than a sudden discontinuity where everything changes in a day. Honestly, I think that's good news, because it gives us some time to see what's happening and respond.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments and training runs take weeks or months, but it does not state that the time models spend doing large-scale test-time computation constrains an overnight explosion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the overnight intelligence explosion idea, the "fast takeoff" scenario, usually rests on this picture where you get an AI that's good enough to do AI research, it improves itself, and then you get this recursive loop that goes vertical in a matter of days or weeks. And I'm skeptical of that for a few reasons.

The first is just that progress has never actually looked like that, even when we've had enormous amounts of compute and talent pointed at a problem. I spent years working on poker and on Diplomacy, and what I saw over and over was that the big jumps came from a small number of real ideas, like scaling test-time compute, like search, and then a huge amount of grinding to make those ideas actually work. The ideas are the bottleneck, and ideas don't come on a schedule. Having more of them in parallel helps, but it doesn't collapse to zero.

The second thing is that there are hard physical constraints. You need compute. You need to run experiments, and experiments take wall-clock time. Even if you had a model tomorrow that was as good as the best researchers at OpenAI, it still has to train models to test its hypotheses, and training runs take weeks and cost a lot of money. Smarter doesn't mean you skip the experiment. In some ways it means you want to run more experiments, not fewer.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that I think a lot of the gains we're going to see are going to be in the form of the models getting much better at reasoning, at thinking for a long time on hard problems. That's real, it's a big deal, and I think it's going to accelerate research. But acceleration is different from an explosion. I think it looks more like what we've already been seeing: things that felt impossible a couple years ago become routine, the cycle keeps compressing, and in retrospect it will look fast. But living through it, it's going to feel like continuous, rapid progress, not a single moment where everything changes overnight.

So I'm not saying this isn't going to be transformative. I actually think it will be. I'm just saying I'd bet on it being a steep curve rather than a discontinuity.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments and training runs take wall-clock time, and mentions reasoning for a long time, but it does not argue that time spent on large-scale test-time computation constrains an overnight intelligence explosion.

astra-6.text:
I think an intelligence explosion is possible. What I’m skeptical of is the claim that it necessarily happens overnight once AI can do AI research.

There’s a big gap between having an idea for a better model and knowing that it actually works. You have to run experiments, and those experiments take compute and time. Even if the researcher is thinking a thousand times faster, the training run doesn’t automatically finish a thousand times faster. And if you need more chips or more power, those have physical lead times.

There’s also the question of diminishing returns. Automating research could produce a huge acceleration, but it doesn’t follow that every improvement makes the next improvement easier. You might be finding increasingly difficult improvements, or running into bottlenecks elsewhere.

So I’d separate ‘AI could dramatically accelerate technological progress’ from ‘AI becomes superintelligent over a weekend.’ The first seems very plausible to me. The second requires additional assumptions about how quickly that feedback loop can run.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments and training runs take time, but it does not identify elapsed time for large-scale test-time computation as a constraint.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we can rule it out, but I’m skeptical of the idea that once an AI can do AI research, everything suddenly happens overnight. That assumes the main bottleneck is coming up with ideas, and that those ideas can immediately turn into a more capable system.

In practice, research involves running experiments, waiting for results, and figuring out which ideas actually work. Even if you could generate a thousand promising ideas in an hour, you’d still need the compute to test them. And if an improvement requires a larger training run or new hardware, those things take time.

So I take the possibility of very rapid progress seriously. I just think there’s a meaningful distinction between AI accelerating research enormously and a self-improvement loop that becomes essentially instantaneous. The first doesn’t automatically imply the second.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments, larger training runs, and new hardware take time, but it does not specifically argue that elapsed time for models to perform large-scale test-time computation constrains an overnight explosion.
